summary: Clioquinol (iodochlorhydroxyquinoline) is a halogenated 8-hydroxyquinoline with antibacterial, antifungal, and antiprotozoal activity. It is now used almost exclusively as a topical agent for inflammatory skin conditions such as infected eczema, intertrigo, and superficial dermatophyte, yeast, and bacterial infections, frequently in fixed combination with a topical corticosteroid (e.g., hydrocortisone). Its oral formulations were withdrawn in many countries in the 1970s after being linked to subacute myelo-optic neuropathy (SMON), a serious neurotoxic syndrome, particularly with high-dose, prolonged oral use. Topical clioquinol can stain skin, hair, and fabrics yellow and may interfere with thyroid function tests because of its iodine content. It should be applied to limited areas for short periods.

moa: Clioquinol is a halogenated 8-hydroxyquinoline whose iodine and chlorine substitutions enhance antimicrobial activity. It acts principally as a chelator of divalent metal cations (notably zinc and copper), disrupting metal-dependent microbial enzyme systems, interfering with microbial membrane and metabolic function, and impairing nucleic acid processes; this confers broad antibacterial, antifungal (including dermatophytes and Candida), and antiprotozoal effects. Applied topically, it exerts a local antimicrobial action on skin pathogens; when combined with a corticosteroid, the steroid suppresses the inflammatory component of the dermatosis while clioquinol addresses secondary infection.

missed: If you forget an application, apply it when you remember. If it is almost time for the next application, skip the missed one and continue your usual schedule. Do not apply extra to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Topical overdose (excessive amount, large areas, or occlusion) increases systemic absorption and the risk of neurotoxicity. Accidental ingestion or large systemic exposure can cause gastrointestinal upset and, historically, neurological toxicity (subacute myelo-optic neuropathy with optic and peripheral nerve damage). Management is to stop use, wash off topical drug, provide supportive care, and seek specialist/poison-centre advice for significant ingestion.
